reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine
clinicalPearls: The commonest and generally mildest form of inherited epidermolysis bullosa, most often autosomal dominant and caused by mutations in the basal keratins KRT5 and KRT14
Blistering occurs within the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis, so the cleavage plane is intraepidermal (above the basement membrane)
Because the split is superficial, blisters tend to heal without scarring or milia, unlike the dystrophic form
Trauma and friction, especially on the hands and feet, provoke blistering, and symptoms are often worse in warm weather
A localised variant affecting mainly the palms and soles and more widespread generalised variants are recognised, with severe forms showing clustered (herpetiform) blistering
Diagnosis is confirmed by immunofluorescence antigen mapping and electron microscopy locating the cleavage plane, with molecular genetic testing
Management is supportive, centred on protecting skin from friction and trauma, wound care, avoidance of overheating, and prevention of secondary infection
reference.pathophysiology: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex is a disorder of the mechanical integrity of the basal layer of the epidermis. Keratins 5 and 14 assemble into the intermediate filament network that gives basal keratinocytes their structural resilience; pathogenic mutations, usually dominant-negative, produce a defective keratin cytoskeleton that cannot withstand mechanical stress. As a result, minor friction or trauma causes the basal cells to rupture and split, so blister formation occurs within the epidermis above the dermo-epidermal junction. Because the basement membrane and dermis remain intact, healing generally proceeds without the scarring characteristic of deeper cleavage-plane disease.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Friction blisters and other mechanobullous conditions
Autoimmune blistering diseases such as bullous pemphigoid
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence antigen mapping to localise the cleavage plane
Transmission electron microscopy of a fresh blister edge
Molecular genetic testing of KRT5 and KRT14
Swabs of blisters or eroded skin when secondary infection is suspected
Family history assessment and genetic counselling
Assessment for extracutaneous involvement in severe subtypes
redFlags: Extensive blistering or erosions with signs of secondary infection or sepsis
Severe generalised involvement in a neonate, prompting reassessment of the subtype
Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty if mucosal involvement occurs in severe variants
Rapidly spreading skin loss suggesting an alternative severe blistering diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most forms, particularly the localised variant, are compatible with a normal life expectancy and improve after childhood, though severe generalised subtypes cause more troublesome blistering; because the cleavage plane is superficial, healing is usually without scarring.
pitfalls: Assuming all epidermolysis bullosa scars, when the simplex form typically heals without scarring
Failing to distinguish it from junctional and dystrophic forms, which have a worse prognosis and deeper cleavage plane
Mistaking neonatal blistering for infection such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Neglecting measures to reduce friction and overheating that precipitate blistering
Overlooking secondary bacterial infection of eroded skin
management: Minimise friction and trauma with soft cushioned footwear, protective padding and measures to stay cool, since heat and mechanical stress provoke blistering
Provide wound care by lancing and draining tense blisters and applying non-adherent dressings, with healing usually free of scarring given the superficial cleavage plane
Treat palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and hyperhidrosis with keratolytics, topical aluminium chloride antiperspirants or botulinum toxin
Control infection by swabbing eroded skin and treating secondary bacterial colonisation
Involve podiatry and foot care to reduce plantar blistering and callus
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant KRT5/KRT14 inheritance and confirm the subtype by antigen mapping and molecular testing
